Motor insurance · South Africa

Retail, market or trade value: which one should your car be insured for?

The right answer is less about picking the biggest number and more about understanding what the policy will actually pay after a theft or write-off.

Quick answer

Choose the value basis you could live with on the day of a total loss, not only the cheapest premium today. Retail usually provides the closest standard route to dealer replacement; market can balance premium and payout; trade gives the lowest baseline and the greatest self-funded gap. Because definitions vary, the coversheet and policy wording must settle the meaning for your specific policy.

Retail, market or trade value can change the premium you pay and the position you are left in if your car is stolen or written off. For most South African drivers who want to replace a car with a similar dealer vehicle, retail value is the strongest standard starting point. Market value is a middle-ground option when its definition is clear. Trade value suits a narrower group who knowingly accept a bigger replacement gap.

The three values describe different positions in the same market

Retail, market and trade values are not three names for one price. They describe different points between what a dealer may pay to acquire a car and what a consumer may pay to buy a comparable dealer-prepared car.

Retail value generally reflects a dealer selling price for a comparable vehicle. Trade value reflects a dealer buy-in or trade-in price. Market value usually sits between them, but its formula is policy-specific: it may mean typical comparable selling prices, an adjusted valuation or a calculation linked to retail and trade. Current explainers from Santam and iWYZE show why the terms should be read in the insurer's own context.

Typical positioning only. Your policy's written definition and settlement clause take priority.
Value basisPlain-English meaningTypical trade-offOften worth considering when
Retail valueWhat a dealer may charge for a comparable car, adjusted for its details and condition.Usually the highest standard insured value and premium, with the strongest replacement position.You want to get closer to dealer replacement cost, especially for a newer or financed car.
Market valueA policy-defined current value, often between retail and trade.Usually a middle position for both premium and potential settlement.You understand the formula and can absorb a moderate difference between settlement and replacement.
Trade valueWhat a dealer may pay to acquire the car for resale.Usually the lowest standard value and premium, with the largest likely replacement gap.The car is older or paid off and you can comfortably fund part of the next car yourself.
Agreed valueA specific amount accepted in advance, subject to the contract and valuation evidence.More certainty about the valuation basis, but eligibility, premium and review conditions can be stricter.The car is classic, rare, modified, restored or poorly represented by standard valuation guides.

That hierarchy helps you compare options, but it does not decide the claim. The next step is to connect the value label to the actual basis of settlement.

The schedule amount may be a ceiling, not a promise

A value on the policy schedule does not automatically mean that exact amount will land in your account. At claim stage, the insurer applies the settlement clause, the car's pre-loss details, the excess and any other contractual deductions.

A useful primary-source example appears in Sasria Circular 497. Its retail-basis example shows a vehicle listed for R500,000, a TransUnion retail value of R455,000 and a R455,000 settlement. Sasria explicitly says its motor cover is a stand-alone policy, so this example should not be applied blindly to an ordinary underlying motor policy. It demonstrates why “whichever is less” wording matters.

If the vehicle is financed, the insurer generally protects the finance house's interest first. The remaining debt can still exceed the insurance settlement because a loan may include interest, fees, a residual or balloon payment; Santam's 2026 consumer guidance highlights this finance-gap risk. A “credit shortfall” or top-up extension may help, but it has its own eligibility rules, exclusions and limits.

This is why a sound policy comparison includes the settlement method and excess, not only the monthly premium.

Which value is the practical fit?

Retail is often the practical default when replacement certainty matters most, market can suit a driver who accepts some shortfall, and trade makes sense only when the lower potential settlement is a deliberate choice. Agreed value belongs in a separate conversation for unusual vehicles.

1

Start with retail if the car is financed

Then compare the current bank settlement, policy value and any credit-shortfall option. Retail reduces risk; it does not erase every finance gap.

2

Consider market if you can fund a gap

Ask the insurer to define market value in writing and show how mileage, condition and local comparable vehicles are treated.

3

Use trade only with open eyes

The saving today should be weighed against the cash you might need to add to replace the car after a total loss.

A car's age is not the only deciding factor. Your cash reserve, finance exposure, the exact derivative, mileage, service history, previous damage and declared accessories can all change the real-world outcome. For a wider view of protection levels, compare third-party and comprehensive car insurance before debating valuation alone.

Your car's exact details shape the valuation

Valuation data is a starting point, not a substitute for identifying the actual vehicle. Two cars with the same badge and registration year can carry different values because of derivative, transmission, mileage, condition, accident history, service record, specification and local demand.

Insurers may use recognised valuation data and then adjust for the individual car. MiWay's current explainer lists make, model, body type, year, mileage, condition, market demand and recent pricing among the factors that can influence vehicle-specific values. iWYZE similarly notes that valuation tools provide an estimated range rather than a permanent figure.

Used-car prices also move. TransUnion reported that in Q4 2024 South African used-vehicle prices were 2.8% lower year on year while new-vehicle prices were 1.7% higher. That dated market snapshot is not a forecast, but it illustrates why original purchase price is a poor long-term proxy for insured value.

Keep the vehicle description current and review the value at renewal. That creates a better base for the settlement conversation if the car is later stolen or declared uneconomical to repair.

Write-off decisions do not follow one universal percentage

A write-off is usually an economic and safety assessment, not the automatic result of crossing one fixed national percentage. The insurer compares repair economics with the pre-loss value and may consider salvage, parts, labour, structural damage and roadworthiness.

Do not build your decision around a social-media claim that “70% damage means a write-off.” Ask how the policy and insurer make the repair-or-total-loss decision. If an accident happens, follow the practical steps in Best Care's South African car-accident guide, preserve evidence and notify the insurer or broker promptly.

If the car is written off, the valuation basis becomes only one line in the final calculation. The car-insurance excess, finance-house interest and applicable policy deductions also matter.

Accessories and modifications need their own line of sight

Non-standard equipment should be disclosed and confirmed in writing rather than assumed to be part of the car's base value. Factory options, aftermarket wheels, canopies, sound systems, tracking equipment, suspension changes and performance modifications may be treated differently.

The official Sasria circular separates retail value, unspecified extras and agreed-value situations, which shows how quickly a generic “my car is worth X” statement can miss the structure of the cover. Your underlying policy may use different rules, but the practical habit is the same: list the item, keep invoices or valuation evidence, and check that the schedule records it correctly.

Important: paying a premium on a high schedule amount does not necessarily create a matching claim entitlement. Avoid both under-insurance and over-insurance by checking the valuation method rather than guessing a number.

A five-minute review can expose the real risk

A useful annual review compares four figures: the insured value, the likely claim basis, the current finance settlement and the cash required to replace the vehicle. If those numbers pull apart, ask questions before renewal rather than after a loss.

  • Confirm the exact make, model, derivative, year, mileage, use and regular driver.
  • Identify whether the schedule says retail, market, trade, agreed or guaranteed value.
  • Read the definition and total-loss settlement clause in the current policy wording.
  • Check the basic and additional excesses that could reduce the net settlement.
  • Get a current settlement letter if the car is financed, including any balloon payment.
  • List accessories and modifications and keep invoices, photographs and valuations.
  • Ask how often the insured value changes and who is responsible for updating it.

If several policies look similar, a broker can help translate the wording and explain the limits of the provider panel. Best Care's guide to using an insurance broker explains that role, while its complete car-insurance guide places valuation alongside cover type, excesses, drivers and claims.

Disagreement starts with evidence, not an argument

If you disagree with a valuation, ask for the figure, source, adjustments and policy clause in writing. Check whether the insurer used the correct derivative, year, mileage, condition and accessories. Then provide relevant evidence, such as service records, dated photographs, invoices, an independent valuation or genuinely comparable vehicles.

Motor disputes are not rare. The National Financial Ombud Scheme reported that motor-vehicle insurance represented 42% of non-life complaints finalised or resolved in 2024. That figure covers many types of motor dispute, not valuation alone, but it reinforces the value of clear records and written explanations.

Use the insurer's internal complaint route first. If the matter remains unresolved and falls within its jurisdiction, the National Financial Ombud Scheme describes its consumer service as free. Best Care also publishes its own complaints process for clients who need a formal route.

Key takeaways

  • Retail value is usually the strongest standard replacement position, but it is not automatically a guaranteed payout.
  • Market value is policy-specific; never assume every insurer uses the same midpoint formula.
  • Trade value can lower the insured value and premium, but it usually leaves the largest replacement or finance gap.
  • A financed car needs two checks: the policy's settlement method and the bank's current settlement balance.
  • The exact derivative, mileage, condition, history, accessories and modifications can affect valuation.
  • Agreed value may suit eligible classic, rare or modified vehicles that standard guides do not describe well.

Frequently asked questions

Is retail value always the best choice for car insurance?

No. Retail value usually offers the strongest standard replacement position, but it can cost more and still does not guarantee a specific payout. The best basis depends on the policy wording, your finance balance, the car's age and what shortfall you could afford.

Is market value the average of retail and trade value?

Sometimes, but not always. Some insurers describe market value as a midpoint, while others use comparable selling prices or an adjusted valuation. Use the definition in your own coversheet and policy wording.

Should a financed car be insured for retail value?

Retail value is often the safer standard starting point for a financed car because it may reduce the replacement gap, but it may still be lower than the finance settlement. Compare a current bank settlement letter with the policy's claim method and ask about credit-shortfall cover.

Will the insurer pay the amount shown on my schedule?

Not necessarily. A schedule amount can be a maximum rather than a guaranteed payment. The insurer may apply the value at the date of loss, the policy's settlement formula, excesses and other deductions unless the contract provides a true agreed or guaranteed value.

What is agreed-value car insurance?

Agreed-value cover uses an amount accepted in advance by the insurer and policyholder, usually for a classic, rare, customised or otherwise hard-to-value car. The valuation evidence, review period, limits and conditions still matter.

How often should I review my car's insured value?

Review it at every renewal and after a material change such as major accessories, restoration, unusual mileage or a finance restructure. Also check that the exact model, derivative, year, mileage and regular use remain accurate.

Are accessories and modifications included automatically?

Do not assume they are. Tell the insurer or broker about factory extras, aftermarket wheels, sound systems, canopies, performance changes and other modifications, then confirm in writing how each item is valued and shown on the schedule.

What can I do if I disagree with a total-loss valuation?

Ask for the written valuation, calculation and policy clause, check the vehicle details and submit evidence such as service records, photographs and comparable listings. Use the insurer's complaints process first, then approach the National Financial Ombud Scheme if the dispute remains unresolved and falls within its jurisdiction.
